requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: When choosing to adopt a DNSBL, a DNSBL user SHOULD keep the following questions in mind:

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: DNSBL users SHOULD consider trial periods and/or ongoing local monitoring of DNSBL suitability.

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: DNSBL users SHOULD periodically check the correct operation of the DNSBL, and cease using DNSBLs that are working incorrectly.

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: The DNSBL user MUST ensure that they understand the intended use of the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: For example, some IP address-based DNSBLs are appropriate for assessment of only the peer IP address of the machine connecting to the DNSBL user's mail server, and not other IP addresses appearing in an email (such as header Received lines or web links) or IRC connections, etc. While a DNSBL user may choose to ignore the intent of the DNSBL, they SHOULD implement any variance in compliance with the DNSBL usage instructions.

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: If you are going to allow a third party's information to guide your filtering decision-making process, you MUST understand the policies and practices of those third parties because responsibility for filter decisions remains ultimately with you, the postmaster.

requirements.heading: Guidance for DNSBL Users
requirements.text: A DNSBL user voluntarily uses the DNSBL data to guide their decisions, and the DNSBL user therefore MUST assume responsibility for dealing with the consequences.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: A DNSBL SHOULD carefully describe the criteria for adding and the criteria for removing an entry from the list.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: Such listing and delisting criteria SHOULD be presented in a clear and readable manner easily accessible to the public on the DNSBL's web site.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: A DNSBL MUST abide by its stated listing and delisting criteria.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: Entries that do not meet the published criteria MUST NOT be added to the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: For example, a DNSBL described as only listing open relays MUST NOT include IP addresses for any other reason.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: Furthermore, the DNSBL documentation SHOULD be clear on the intended use of the DNSBL -- whether it be intended for peer addresses of email, IRC, etc.

requirements.heading: Transparency
requirements.text: Availability of documentation concerning a DNSBL SHOULD NOT be dependent on the continued operation of DNS for DNSBL queries.

requirements.heading: Listing/Delisting Criteria SHOULD Be Easily Available
requirements.text: Listing and delisting criteria for DNSBLs SHOULD be easily available and SHOULD be located in a place clearly marked in its own section of the web site affiliated with the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Listing/Delisting Criteria SHOULD Be Easily Available
requirements.text: This additional technical information can confuse end users, so a separate page, section, or query function on its own SHOULD be dedicated to detailing why a specific entry appears in the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Audit Trail SHOULD Be Maintained
requirements.text: A DNSBL SHOULD maintain an audit trail for all listings, and it is RECOMMENDED that it is made publicly available in an easy to find location, preferably on the DNSBL's web site.

requirements.heading: Audit Trail SHOULD Be Maintained
requirements.text: For example, a DNSBL operator MAY make the audit trail data selectively accessible in such a way as to not disclose information that might assist spammers, such as the location or identity of a spam trap.

requirements.heading: The Scope and Aggressiveness of Listings MUST Be Disclosed
requirements.text: Therefore, DNSBL listing policies MUST include statements as to the scope and aggressiveness of listings and include, as appropriate, whether the DNSBL operator intends the listings to be used in scoring or other techniques.

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: Generally speaking, listings SHOULD be considered temporary and should expire on their own at some point in the future, unless reasons for listing still exist.

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: Expiration intervals SHOULD be chosen to be reasonable for the type of listing.

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: DNSBLs based on relatively static information, such as block assignment or domain names of demonstrably bad actors, MAY have very long expiration intervals or be removed only upon request after verification that the removal criteria have been met.

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: Manually created DNSBL entries SHOULD be periodically reviewed in some manner.

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: It is RECOMMENDED that DNSBL operators publish in general terms their expiration policy, even if it's only "delist on request" or "no expiration is performed".

requirements.heading: Listings SHOULD Be Temporary
requirements.text: In information-only lists, a method for users requesting corrections to the information (if appropriate) SHOULD be published.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: Discussions about whether a DNSBL should remove an entry MAY include activity in a public forum.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: Methods for processing removal requests through private, direct exchanges, such as person-to-person email or a combination of web page requests and email responses, SHOULD be available.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: As a minimum, the DNSBL SHOULD have a web page that has a removal request function (separate from the page describing listing criteria as per Section 2.1.1).

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: The DNSBL SHOULD also make available an email address to handle issues other than blocking issues.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: The DNSBL operator MUST NOT use the list in question in such a way that removal requests would be blocked; and moreover, the operator SHOULD make mailboxes available in order to allow affected users to submit their requests.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: If filtering should be necessary in such circumstances, filtering methods with as low false positive rate as practical SHOULD be chosen.

requirements.heading: A Direct Non-Public Way to Request Removal SHOULD Be Available
requirements.text: DNSBL operators SHOULD be prepared to provide alternate means of contact in case of system failure due to DDoS (distributed denial-of- service) attack or other reasons.

requirements.heading: Response SHOULD Be Prompt
requirements.text: A response to removal requests or queries about a listing SHOULD be prompt.

requirements.heading: Response SHOULD Be Prompt
requirements.text: A DNSBL operator SHOULD respond within 2 days and MUST respond within 7 days, except in the case that the DNSBL operator has deemed that further discussion of the issue will not result in meeting the conditions for removal and has notified the requestor of that decision.

requirements.heading: Response SHOULD Be Prompt
requirements.text: A DNSBL MAY impose restrictions on who (e.g., a network operator's representative or domain name owner) may make valid removal requests.

requirements.heading: Response SHOULD Be Prompt
requirements.text: However, in many DNSBLs, this is inadvisable because it requires impractical amounts of effort; hence, it is NOT RECOMMENDED in most cases.

requirements.heading: A Given DNSBL SHOULD Have Similar Criteria for Listing and
requirements.text: The criteria for being removed from a DNSBL SHOULD bear a reasonable relationship to the factors that were the cause of the addition to the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: A Given DNSBL SHOULD Have Similar Criteria for Listing and
requirements.text: If a listed entity fulfills all published requirements for removal from a DNSBL, then the DNSBL operator SHOULD NOT impose any additional obstacles to remove a given entry from the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: A Given DNSBL SHOULD Have Similar Criteria for Listing and
requirements.text: There SHOULD NOT be any extra rules for delisting other than the ones listed in the published listing criteria.

requirements.heading: Conflict of Interest
requirements.text: Therefore, negative-connotation DNSBLs MUST not charge fees or require donations for delisting or "faster handling", and it is RECOMMENDED that such DNSBLs that do charge fees or require donations not be used.

requirements.heading: DNSBL Query Root Domain Name SHOULD be a Subdomain
requirements.text: The DNSBL "query root" SHOULD be below the registered domain name, so that the DNSBL information is not conflated with domain name housekeeping information (e.g., name server or MX records) for the domain name.

requirements.heading: DNSBL Query Root Domain Name SHOULD be a Subdomain
requirements.text: It is RECOMMENDED that, even if there is a single DNSBL zone with entry type distinguished by return code, separate subdomain names (of the query root) consist only of the corresponding entries.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Be Adequately Provisioned
requirements.text: The DNSBL SHOULD have sufficient name server capacity to handle the expected loading and have sufficient redundancy to handle normal outages.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Be Adequately Provisioned
requirements.text: Name servers SHOULD provide appropriate glue records, possibly in different Top-Level Domains (TLDs) to protect against single-TLD issues.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Be Adequately Provisioned
requirements.text: If the DNSBL offers zone transfers (in addition to or instead of standard DNSBL query mechanisms), it SHOULD be sufficiently provisioned to handle the expected loading.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Be Adequately Provisioned
requirements.text: Provisioning SHOULD take the likelihood of this into account and include plans for dealing with it.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: In the absence of new emerging standards, it is RECOMMENDED that domain-name-based DNSBLs use a test entry of "test".

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: Further, in Section 3.5, DNSBL operators MUST NOT list 127.0.0.1.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: Therefore, a positive listing for 127.0.0.1 SHOULD indicate that the DNSBL has started listing the world and is non-functional.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: Similarly, a domain-based DNSBL SHOULD NOT ever list the reserved domain INVALID, and a positive listing for INVALID SHOULD indicate that the DNSBL is non- functional.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: This operational flag usage and meaning SHOULD be published on the DNSBL's web site, and the DNSBL user SHOULD periodically test the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs SHOULD Provide Operational Flags
requirements.text: Some mail systems are unable to differentiate between these various results or flags, however, so a public DNSBL SHOULD NOT include opposing or widely different meanings -- such as 127.0.0.23 for "sends good mail" and 127.0.0.99 for "sends bad mail" -- within the same DNS zone.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: The DNSBL operator MUST issue impending shutdown warnings (on the DNSBL web site, appropriate mailing lists, newsgroups, vendor newsletters, etc.), and indicate that the DNSBL is inoperative using the signaling given in Section 3.3.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: Only after these warnings have been issued for a significant period of time (RECOMMENDED: one or more months), should the DNSBL operator finally shutdown the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: MUST NOT list the entire Internet

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: SHOULD shed the DNSBL query load from the DNSBL name servers, permitting the registered domain name to continue being usable.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: SHOULD, perhaps through increased delays, indicate to the mail administrator that the DNSBL is no longer functional.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: Name server or query lookups MUST NOT be aimed at third parties unrelated to DNSBL operation.

requirements.heading: Shutdowns MUST Be Done Gracefully
requirements.text: The base domain name SHOULD be registered indefinitely, so as to prevent the domain name from being a "booby trap" for future owners, and/or to prevent a new owner from maliciously listing the entire Internet.

requirements.heading: Listing of Special and Reserved IP Addresses MUST Be Disclosed
requirements.text: The DNSBL MAY list loopback, [RFC1918], LINK-LOCAL class [RFC3927], class D/E, and any other permanently reserved or special-use IP addresses [RFC5735] (and [RFC5156] for IPv6).

requirements.heading: Listing of Special and Reserved IP Addresses MUST Be Disclosed
requirements.text: Such use MUST be disclosed in the documentation related to the DNSBL.

requirements.heading: Listing of Special and Reserved IP Addresses MUST Be Disclosed
requirements.text: As additional insurance against listings of space that should not be listed through testing or other unforeseen events, DNSBL operators SHOULD consider implementing facilities to prevent them.

requirements.heading: Listing of Special and Reserved IP Addresses MUST Be Disclosed
requirements.text: A functioning DNSBL MUST NOT list 127.0.0.1.

requirements.heading: Considerations for DNSBLs Listing Insecure Hosts
requirements.text: The following recommendations for such DNSBLs MAY help alleviate this risk.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs MUST NOT Scan without Provocation
requirements.text: DNSBLs MUST NOT automatically probe for insecure hosts without provocation.

requirements.heading: DNSBLs MUST NOT Scan without Provocation
requirements.text: Therefore, scanning MUST be targeted, rather than broad-based, where a given scan is motivated by a specific reason to have concern about the address being scanned.

requirements.heading: Re-Scan Periods SHOULD Be Reasonable
requirements.text: If the DNSBL operator re-scans a host in order to determine whether the listing SHOULD time out or not, the re-scan period SHOULD be reasonable.

requirements.heading: Re-Scan Periods SHOULD Be Reasonable
requirements.text: Automated scanning SHOULD NOT occur more often than once every 24 hours.

requirements.heading: Re-Scan Periods SHOULD Be Reasonable
requirements.text: It is RECOMMENDED that automated re-scanning should cease within a reasonable period of the vulnerability no longer existing and of the targeting conditions no longer being met.

requirements.heading: Scans MUST NOT Be Destructive
requirements.text: Scanning methodologies MUST NOT negatively impact the scanned host.

requirements.heading: Removals SHOULD Be Possible in Absence of the DNSBL Operator
requirements.text: If removals cannot be automated (e.g., via robot re-testing or self- removal), then the DNSBL SHOULD have multiple administrators so that a removal request can be processed if the principal list administrator is on vacation or otherwise unavailable.

requirements.heading: Protect against Misconfiguration/Outages
requirements.text: DNSBL users MUST test their initial DNSBL configurations to ensure that they're working correctly and SHOULD periodically recheck the status of the DNSBLs they use and adjust their configuration as necessary.

requirements.heading: Protect against Misconfiguration/Outages
requirements.text: While in many cases it can be difficult to detect such situations, to protect against such misconfiguration, it is RECOMMENDED that DNSBL operators make design decisions to mitigate the impact of such mistakes and make efforts to contact administrative contacts to remedy the situation where appropriate.

requirements.heading: Protect against Misconfiguration/Outages
requirements.text: But the DNSBL operator SHOULD also prepare to take appropriate steps to protect the operational infrastructure (e.g., have the ability to block abusive users from causing further damage).

requirements.heading: Protect against Misconfiguration/Outages
requirements.text: Appropriate use of the DNSBL SHOULD be documented on the web site.

requirements.heading: Error Handling
requirements.text: Therefore, DNSBLs SHOULD have policies and procedures in place to treat operational problems conservatively, be prepared to mass purge dubious entries, prevent future erroneous entries, and notify their users by the DNSBL's web page.

requirements.heading: Security Considerations
requirements.text: DNSBL users SHOULD be prepared to periodically test the DNSBLs they use for correct operation.
